name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPS-9 'Rattler'
description:
The KPS-9 Rattler is the cheapest submachine gun on GLMZ. At Φ400, it costs less than many handguns, and Kang-Petrov manufactures it with that price point as the primary design constraint. The weapon is a simple blowback-operated SMG chambered in 9mm brass-cased, with a stamped steel receiver, polymer grip, and a 32-round stick magazine. There is no BCI link, no electronic sight, no onboard computer. The sights are molded into the receiver.

Reliability is inconsistent. The Rattler functions adequately when clean and properly lubricated, but the loose tolerances that enable mass production also admit contamination. In dusty or wet conditions, malfunctions increase noticeably. The weapon's accuracy is sufficient for engagements inside 50 meters, but beyond that distance the combination of fixed sights and a short barrel makes consistent hits challenging.

None of this matters to the Rattler's customers. The KPS-9 exists because violence is not exclusively a privilege of the well-funded. For Φ400, a person in a Tier 1 zone gets a weapon that fires 30 rounds of commonly available ammunition. It is not a good weapon. It is an available weapon. In a world where availability often matters more than quality, the Rattler sells millions.
specifications:
caliber: 9mm brass-cased
effective_range: 50m
rate_of_fire: 600 rpm (cyclic)
magazine_capacity: 32 rounds
weight: 2.1 kg
tactical_use: The Rattler has no tactical sophistication. It is a volume-of-fire weapon used at close range where accuracy is determined by proximity rather than skill. In desperate defense scenarios, the KPS-9 provides suppressive capability that a handgun cannot match. Its sole tactical advantage is ubiquity — ammunition and spare parts are available everywhere, and the weapon's simplicity means anyone can learn to operate it in minutes.
cultural_context: The Rattler is the weapon of the desperate, the impoverished, and the unprepared. Finding a KPS-9 in someone's possession tells you nothing about their affiliations — it tells you about their budget. The weapon appears in crime scenes, defensive actions, and everywhere that violence occurs among people who cannot afford better. Kang-Petrov has been criticized for manufacturing a weapon this cheap, but the alternative is a monopoly on violence by those who can afford premium arms.
story_hooks: A bulk shipment of 10,000 Rattlers was intercepted en route to a Tier 1 zone that is about to vote on corporate annexation. The timing suggests someone wants the vote to go a specific way.
A forensic analyst has traced identical manufacturing defects in Rattlers from three different crime scenes — the weapons came from the same production batch, suggesting coordinated distribution.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian, almost crude submachine gun with a boxy receiver and minimal ergonomic refinement. The Rattler has the compressed, no-frills silhouette of a weapon designed for cost rather than elegance—squared-off edges, a stubby barrel, and an overall impression of purposeful brutality stripped of pretense.
physical_description.dimensions: Length: 38 cm (stock collapsed), Barrel length: 10.2 cm, Width: 5.8 cm across receiver
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty but manageable—2.1 kg feels substantial in one hand but not unwieldy. The mass is concentrated forward around the stamped receiver, creating a nose-heavy balance that demands control rather than finesse.
physical_description.primary_material: Stamped steel receiver with minimal machining; polymer grip frame and furniture.
physical_description.finish: Matte parkerized steel with visible mill marks and stamping artifacts. The surface is deliberately rough—no polish, no shine, designed to shed light and avoid reflection. Worn spots expose bare metal where lubricant has been wiped away.
physical_description.color_scheme: Industrial gunmetal gray with flat black polymer accents. No branding flourish—the finish is functional, not aesthetic.
physical_description.grip_texture: Bare polymer, textured only enough for functional traction. Slightly tacky, with fine molding lines visible. The grip is narrow and angular—designed to fit many hands adequately rather than any hand well.
distinctive_features: Fixed iron sights molded directly into the receiver—crude, notched post front and peep rear
Visible stamping seams along the receiver body where pressed steel panels meet
A 32-round stick magazine with witness holes every four rounds, marked in faded white paint
Simple hammer-fired mechanism visible through cocking port
Oversized safety lever—purely mechanical, requires deliberate movement
Heat stress marks around the barrel collar from repetitive fire
Slight patina of old cosmoline in the receiver corners
Loose-fitting dust cover that rattles slightly when shaken
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Stamped markings on the right receiver: 'KANG-PETROV ARMS' and 'KPS-9' in plain sans-serif font, no logo embellishment. Caliber stamp '9MM' on the barrel. Serial number punched into the receiver above the trigger guard in five digits—no special formatting.
physical_description.condition_typical: Appears well-used but maintained. Lubricant residue in the receiver, minor scratches on the stock, slight finish wear on edges from handling. Not pristine, but functional—the weapon of someone who actually shoots it rather than displays it.
